summary:
# NOTES: *A Prince of Good Fellows* (Robert Barr, 1902; McClure, Phillips & Co., New York; illus. Edmund J. Sullivan)

**Front matter:** Also by Barr: *In the Midst of Alarms*, *Tekla*. Frontispiece: "JACOBUS, V, REX, SCOTORUM. THE PRINCE OF GOOD FELLOWS." Dedicated to Thomas Spencer Jerome, Villa of the Castle, Capri. Copyright 1901/1902. Published May 1902.

**Contents (page):** 1 The King Intervenes (1); 2 The King Dines (29); 3 The King's Tryst (47); 4 The King Investigates (77); 5 The King's Gold (113); 6 The King A-Begging (147); 7 The King's Visit (185); 8 The King Explores (213); 9 The King Drinks (243); 10 The King Sails (269); 11 The King Weds (297).

Protagonist: James V, King of Scotland (age 22 at ch.3; 26 at ch.11). Alias: "Guidman / Master / Laird of Ballengeich" (farmer disguise). Mostly called "the king", "James", "Jamie".

---

## 1. THE KING INTERVENES
- Stirling at dusk. Young man in grey check plaid, coarse bonnet (= James in disguise as Ballengeich).
- Mounted court noble strikes him with whip, nearly trampled. He presses to wall, hand reaches for hip (no weapon), removes bonnet.
- Visits cobbler **Flemming** in shuttered lower-town shop. "Hey, guidman!" Ballengeich: "a fair exchange" (bed/stall arrangement).
- Ballengeich claims to be the king's enemy. Flemming reveals conspiracy: 11 men (plus Flemming = 12, "Apostles") meet in his shop, Wednesdays 11 pm. Plan: kidnap James, hold him in a house, force reform.
- Ballengeich's house: stone, on a hill near Stirling, could withstand siege.
- Ballengeich warns: "Word of a Stuart" is worthless. Mentions James escaping Falkland (Earl of Angus's stronghold) at age 16.
- Flemming: "between the cart-wheel and the hard road", "two hashings". Ballengeich offers plan: a deputation with safe conduct signed by king, eleven persons, Flemming as spokesman.
- Wednesday meeting: leader at head of table; oath given; plan accepted; Ballengeich becomes 12th member.
- Safe conduct for eleven arrives via Ballengeich; delivered to Flemming.
- Conference Wednesday noon. Eleven searched in courtyard, locked in room with oak table, throne chair. King enters frowning: "There is a chair for each of you; sit down." Says he chose Wednesday to end their "rebellious gatherings"; "the word of a Stuart... it is a pity I should not take advantage of it."
- Bell; block under black cloth; masked executioner with axe. "This is the entertainment I have provided."
- Flemming protests safe conduct; king: "Safe conduct to where?"
- Flemming offers himself alone; leader: "No, by God... We stand together, or fall together."
- King: "Headsman, do your duty." Headsman reveals box with jug and eleven drinking-horns. King laughs: "I frightened you, Flemming... I'll wager my gold crown against a weaver's woollen bonnet." Wine praised.
- King's toast: "May there never come a time when a Scotchman is afraid to risk his head for what he thinks is right."

## 2. THE KING DINES
- Sir **Donald Sinclair** and **Archbishop of St. Andrews** discuss king: archbishop "my wame's beginning to think my throat's cut" (empty larder); calls James "a nought posing as a nine."
- King angry at empty larder; orders **chief huntsman** (woodlander) brought in, thrown into room.
- Huntsman reports venison seized at **Arnprior** by **John Buchanan**: "if James was king in Stirling, John was king in Kippen."
- **Ronald of the Hills** (red-haired Highlander, Gaelic only, drew arrow) tied up.
- King appoints Ronald chief huntsman to the kitchen after Gaelic exchange via **MacNeish**. King cuts Ronald's bonds with sword. Ronald shouts "Loch Sloy!" and kisses king's buckle. MacNeish: "Gratitude in a MacFarlane!"
- Archbishop: "if the Buchanans are drunk"; king: "we will sober them."
- Ride to Arnprior via Ballengeich path, ~20 soldiers. Sir Donald: "The king! The king!" Gate taken.
- Hall: pipers playing "Buchanan for ever." King's sword at Buchanan's neck: "As you get north of Stirling, Buchanan, it is customary to bring the knife with you when you go out to dine." Weapons heaped.
- "Insult... or... desired to become his cook?" Buchanan: honour of "grace my humble board." King: "I was sure of it."
- Buchanan made cup-bearer. Toast: "King of Kippen," "Scotland including Kippen." Buchanan hungry at the end.

## 3. THE KING'S TRYST
- Background: peace with England, friendly with France, pledged to French bride. Great-grandfather James II crushed Black Douglas; James scattered Red Douglas (Angus) to exile.
- Hunting NW of Stirling. Woman **Catherine** emerges from forest: "my lord, the king." Tirewoman to **Lady Margaret Stuart** (king's mother) at Methven. Ruddy-gold hair, deep blue eyes, firm mouth.
- Message: mother at **Doune** castle; wants secret visit; constable **Stuart** of Doune (king's friend, younger brother of mother's husband) should not know. King: mother hasn't written in a year; "quarrelled with her third husband."
- Catherine: "I have been a gentlewoman, sire." Meeting at new bridge over the Teith.
- King dismisses retinue, rides after her; walks to Doune. Postern door, rope ladder, turret stair. Room with tapestry work.
- Catherine locks him in. King breaks a bench against the larger door. **Isabel** (Catherine's twin, dressed as lady) enters with huge key.
- Isabel reveals mother's marriages: Margaret Tudor (1), Margaret Stuart (2), Margaret Douglas (3, wife of Earl of Angus), Margaret Stuart again, spouse of Lord Methven (4), owner of Doune. Isabel and Catherine are Douglases; uncle Archibald Douglas, Earl of Angus.
- Catherine, dagger in hand, vows to kill king: "perjured soul shall find exit through a postern gate." Isabel weeps, pleads.
- King mocks, calmly debates; cites James I (Catherine Douglas, 1437, arm shattered in door). Cites Boyds, James III, Black Douglas; "assassination... very rarely accomplishes its object."
- King reveals his own dagger. Takes key, steps out, bolts women into stairway.
- Women weep. King re-enters, offers: rescind father's exile; right to live in own castle; safe conduct to England; remain at Doune. Refuses to rescind Angus's banishment.
- Catherine: "We ask nothing but... leaving the country." Isabel: "I go with my sister and my mother."
- King kisses Catherine's hand: "My fair antagonist, I bid you good-night." Kisses Isabel on lips.

## 4. THE KING INVESTIGATES
- Border: English courier complains of raids. Nobles debate. **Earl of Bothwell** pleads for Borderers. **Lord Maxwell**: "hang the English envoy." **Adam Scott of Tushielaw** and **Cockburn of Henderland** threaten to side with raiders. King: "That is treason"; calls Scott "King of the Border."
- King consults **Sir David Lyndsay** ("Davie," poet); Lyndsay undecided. Sir Donald reports Scott and Cockburn fled; Bothwell, Home, Maxwell, Fairniherst, Johnston, Buccleuch closeted together.
- King summons **Flemming**, calls him "Solomon." Flemming: "leave them alone," Lyndsay agrees.
- Plan: three disguised as cattle-drovers ("honest cattle merchants"). Flemming is purse-bearer; Lyndsay handles costumes. Flemming: "I'm no horseman."
- Three ride Border; fail at cattle talk. Inn of **Armstrong** (landlord). **Johnny Armstrong** arrives with six men, ties up the three: "You are spies."
- King: "twenty pounds Scots" (for a stirk). Johnny: "I am Johnny Armstrong... You have to learn that Johnny, and not Jamie, is king of the Border."
- Stronghold on rock over river; tower; cattle; gallows-beam with hanged man. **Peter** cuts body down. Armstrong's invention: water-powered screw lift (pine-tree screw, platform, three cords).
- Prisoners in tower-top room; one prisoner says "They hanged my mate."
- Escape: Flemming waxes a rope with a ball of wax from pocket. King: "if that lets us escape, I'll knight you." Lyndsay: "beheaded" joke. Guide prisoner goes first, king last. Escape by river.
- Reprisal: king orders Cockburn and Scott beheaded; Bothwell to Edinburgh Castle; Maxwell, Home, Fairniherst, Johnston, Buccleuch imprisoned. Sir Donald supplies troops.
- King returns to inn with 20 troopers; Sir Donald sends for Armstrong. Armstrong comes with 40 men; surrounded; "Trapped!"
- Armstrong pleads: offers service, gold. King refuses. Armstrong's prophecy: "as sure as this day is the fatal thirteenth" (13 years).
- "The forty-one trees bore their burden." (41 hanged.)

## 5. THE KING'S GOLD
- Italian alchemist **Signor Farini** (secretly a Frenchman, per king) in abandoned refectory of Stirling monastery. Claims to make gold from earth.
- Lyndsay meets king in street (Lyndsay has money). King and Lyndsay enter; **Master of Ballengeich** (king) with Lyndsay; warder refuses; king threatens warrant. Five gold pieces each.
- Experiment: crucible, bellows imps, scarlet-robed Farini. Doubles/trebles returned. Nobles keep staking; Farini's gold fails; threats of swords.
- King secretly suspects French ambassador's bribery; coins marked "F" (king's mint, from French ambassador's bullion). "Flodden" motive.
- King tells Lyndsay to raise stakes so the "goose lays golden eggs."
- Farini claims wing-flight invention; king demands demonstration at Stirling cliff. Farini confesses; French ambassador pushes him: "Fly, you fool!" Farini falls, thigh broken. Ambassador ships him to France (via Leith). King winks at Lyndsay.

## 6. THE KING A-BEGGING
- King's poem "The Beggar Man" (13 stanzas). Shows Flemming; debate: beggar happier than king.
- Flemming praises poem; compares to Gavin Douglas. King hates Douglas name. Flemming praises Lyndsay; king reveals Lyndsay married Janet Douglas.
- Nobles' petition; king gives "this day fortnight."
- King disguises as beggar, leaves farmer clothes with Flemming; belt of gold; sets off alone for a week.
- Storm; wayside inn in Torwood Forest. Landlord; king's threat: "matchlock." King barricades room. Next morning landlord sends boy **Jock** to **Steenie** and men.
- Five ruffians attack at second turning; king breaks wrist of one, cracks crown of another. Giant **Baldy Hutchinson** rescues.
- Baldy to hang at **St. Ninians** (Friday). Relative of Douglases; called king "damn him"; letter to weavers' plot; eleven plotters.
- King: "I am the king." Baldy thinks he's mad. King to St. Ninians.
- Sheriff: "crazy cobbler again" (Flemming arrives, begs). King on scaffold: "I am James, King of Scotland... The king reprieves Baldy Hutchinson." Flemming: "God save the King!"
- Mob riot; sheriff pushes king down. Baldy wrenches scaffold cross-bar. Trooper **MacKenzie** rides for troops.
- **Sir Donald Sinclair** arrives; king: "Halt, Sir Donald!" Sheriff kneels. Baldy waves to crowd.

## 7. THE KING'S VISIT
- Highlanders (~20, pipers) storm Stirling; disarmed by guard. Leader **Finlay MacNab**, "fifth of my name," of Glendochart/Loch Tay. Interpreter **MacPherson** (insulted: "Touch not the Cat"; MacPherson = Chattan branch).
- MacNab's grievance: Robert the Bruce destroyed MacNab parchments and lands; Battle of Del Rhi.
- King restores MacNab's sword. MacNab invites king: "Jamie, my lad... come visit me at Loch Tay." King agrees.
- Stirling banquet; Burgundy wine; MacNab's arms with motto "Timor omnis abseto." Clansmen cut goblets with swords.
- King visits Loch Tay with Pope's legate, Spanish, French ambassadors. Castle of logs (pine). Dinner under trees.
- King knights MacNab ("Sir Finlay"). Night farewell: bugle blasts; torches; men slide down from walls; castle burned. "A monarch's pathway must be lighted."

## 8. THE KING EXPLORES
- James MacDonald of Sleat (son of laird of Sleat) boasts of winning a lady and calls king's crown the only advantage; calls for swords. Treason; held hostage at Stirling. King tolerant.
- King plans visit to Skye; **Allaster Crottach** (MacLeod of Dunvegan, humpback; charter 15 June 1468, king's charter 13 Feb; galley of 26 oars).
- MacDonald disappears from Stirling; goes to Doune, then with king.
- Fleet ordered to Loch Torridon. Two young men sail in fishing-boat with gillies; harbour named **Portree** ("Haven of the King").
- Boatbuilder **Malcolm MacLeod** built the 26-oared galley ("King's barge"). Gaelic poet recites epic.
- Malcolm at Dunvegan rivalry; Malcolm's daughter (Miss MacLeod) appears in later chapters.
- King's proclamation (Great Seal, Gaelic) praises Malcolm MacLeod's boat. Malcolm delighted: "E-god, the king knows a good boat."
- Poetry contest: king places 15th. King irritated; MacDonald reports.
- Dunvegan invites them; horses and escort.

## 9. THE KING DRINKS
- Ride to Dunvegan, 7 leagues. Pipers from MacRimmon College at Bocraig, Loch Follart. Dunvegan Castle; new massive tower under construction.
- Rooms separated; king calls himself "Guidman of Ballengeich," "small farmer." MacLeod: "I heard you were prisoner at Stirling?" MacDonald angry.
- Signature check on king's proclamation; MacDonald affirms genuine. MacLeod threatens spies. King: "Are you a rebel against your king, MacLeod of Skye?" King orders MacLeod to be seated.
- Dinner: MacLeod's three flagons challenge ("empty... at a draught"). Stretcher-bearers. King: "May he be blest with more wisdom than were some of his ancestors!" Gillies swoop stretcher; king falls: "Unfair, by Saint Andrew, unfair!"

## 10. THE KING SAILS
- Next morning: MacDonald proposes demanding passage; king proposes coercion. Gillie follows; chanter whistle; dozen armed men block road. Return.
- Study: MacLeod's daughter (19-20, unnamed; "Miss MacLeod") with broken English; king flirts; MacDonald speaks Gaelic, excluding king.
- MacLeod: "Are you... emissaries of the king?" Parole terms: no escape, no communication with Stirling. King amends: shall not leave island without knowledge.
- MacDonald proposes marriage to Miss MacLeod; plan via Malcolm, with letter to fleet.
- Fleet sails up Loch Follart. King demands "twenty-six oared barge." MacLeod: "Bring round the king's barge... I myself will take the rudder."
- Daughter pleads in Gaelic; king grants her request if she and MacDonald accompany him to Stirling; gives her hand to MacDonald. MacLeod taken to Stirling.

## 11. THE KING WEDS
- James (26) departs for France (January) to marry **Mary of Vendome** (daughter of Duc de Vendome; reported beautiful; wealthy).
- Arrival at Falaise/Loches castle; Constable **Talbot** of Falaise; "Pearl of France." Talbot loves Mary. King: "I came... bought another nor sold myself."
- Loches: **Francis I** greets king warmly; news of Charles's army broken in Provence.
- Mary: pale, sickly, mother **Duchesse de Vendome** controls her. King despairs.
- Garden: **Madeleine de Montmorency** (~17) drops handkerchief; king climbs tree, kisses her hand; she says Mary loves Talbot. Second meeting: king kisses her thrice. Francis enraged, then approves: "I cannot marry Mary of Vendome"; "She is but a child." Madeleine: "I am fully seventeen."
- Ends: "James the Fifth of Scotland married the fair Madeleine of France."

---

## Appended advertisements (separate books)

**A. *The Hound of the Baskervilles*** by A. Conan Doyle, "A Sherlock Holmes Novel," illus. Sidney Paget. Review in *The London Chronicle*, headed "THE ZENITH OF SHERLOCK HOLMES." Footnote quote: "I tell you, Watson, this time we have a foeman who is worthy of our steel." Price $1.25. McClure, Phillips & Co.

**B. *The House with the Green Shutters*** by George Douglas. "First novel of a new master." Eighth edition, $1.50. Reviews: *London Times* ("Worthy of the hand that drew 'Weir of Hermiston'"); *The Spectator* ("Zola and Balzac"); *Vanity Fair* ("AEschylean tragedy"); *Harper's Weekly* ("If Thomas Hardy had written of Scotland..."). McClure, Phillips & Co.
